For example, someone learning photography through online critiques and editing software. Too much time watching advice can replace the actual practice that creates skill. The change is substantial, although it has not affected every group in the same way.
answers.alternative_a: Technology has turned many private hobbies into social or even commercial activities. People share progress, find niche communities and sometimes sell what they make. For example, a home baker building an online audience and taking occasional orders. Public metrics can reduce enjoyment if every hobby begins to feel like a performance. The change is substantial, although it has not affected every group in the same way.
answers.alternative_b: It has created entirely new leisure activities. Gaming, digital art and virtual communities offer forms of creativity and competition that did not exist before. For example, friends meeting weekly inside an online strategy game. Screen-based hobbies should not be dismissed, although balance with physical and offline activity still matters. The change is substantial, although it has not affected every group in the same way.

answers.ta_route: To some extent, yes, but it is not a universal rule. The main reason is hobbies protect identity from being defined entirely by work, since absorbing activity interrupts worry and restores attention. For example, reading for pleasure after work. The effect can be significant when the pattern becomes routine. However, some productive hobbies are genuinely satisfying, so I would describe it as a tendency rather than a rule.
answers.alternative_a: In many cases, yes. The main reason is leisure does not need to be productive to be valuable, since play creates intrinsic motivation. For example, photography shifting from observation to constant gear purchases. The effect can be significant when the pattern becomes routine. However, free time varies sharply by job and caregiving, so I would describe it as a tendency rather than a rule.
answers.alternative_b: Not necessarily; there is a strong counterargument. The counterpoint is that technology can widen access while adding more screen use. In some settings, hobbies become expensive when equipment and status replace the activity, but the outcome depends on design and behaviour. For example, balcony gardening using simple reused containers. That example shows why a simple yes-or-no answer can miss the conditions that determine the result.
